documents.title: Guidelines on using Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) for Coursework
documents.summary: Undergraduate college policy: GenAI is disallowed by default, instructors decide per course and are encouraged to state their policy in the syllabus, and any permitted use must be acknowledged under the Academic Honor Policy. Sample acknowledgment statements are included.
documents.stance_why: The college policy sets a default ban ("Students may not use GenAI tools for submitted coursework unless expressly permitted") but expressly gives each instructor authority to allow or disallow AI ("Instructors may either allow or disallow"). Because the operative decision is delegated to instructors and the default is only a fallback, the document is coded delegates.

units.why: The summary states "instructors have authority to determine whether AI tools may be used in their course", so the rule is set per instructor (P04), addressed to instructors; P04 fits better than P01 because the college itself sets no uniform permission here.
units.anchor: instructors have authority to determine whether AI tools may be used in their course
units.policy: Instructors have authority to determine whether AI tools may be used in their course.

units.why: The summary ties the Academic Honor Policy to "student use of GenAI tools in submitted work requires appropriate acknowledgment", a disclosure duty on students (P24).
units.anchor: student use of GenAI tools in submitted work requires appropriate acknowledgment

units.why: This sentence defines GenAI ("a powerful branch of artificial intelligence that focuses on creating new content"), which sets what the policy covers (P61), so it is informational for all.
units.anchor: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is a powerful branch of artificial intelligence that focuses on creating
units.policy: Generative AI is defined as a branch of artificial intelligence that creates new content such as text, image or audio.

units.why: The passage notes GenAI is "integrated by software vendors into many common applications ... including word processing, coding, and data analysis software", acknowledging AI built into everyday software (P07); informational only, so neutral.
units.anchor: These tools have also been integrated by software vendors into many common applications used in
units.policy: These tools have also been integrated by software vendors into many common applications used in academic settings, including word processing, coding, and data analysis software.

units.why: The statement "unrestricted usage is neither always nor necessarily appropriate to the college learning environment" gives the institution-level framing for limits on AI (P56); no specific rule is set, so informs/neutral.
units.anchor: unrestricted usage is neither always nor necessarily appropriate to the college learning environment

units.why: "Academic integrity is a core value of our academic community" and GenAI "can at times also compromise that value" is a principle-level framing of the policy's purpose (P56).
units.anchor: Academic integrity is a core value of our academic community

units.why: This is the headline rule: "Students may not use GenAI tools for submitted coursework unless expressly permitted", a default ban on graded work, so P01; P06 (silent syllabus) is covered by the separate 'disallowed by default' sentence.
units.anchor: Students may not use GenAI tools for submitted coursework unless expressly permitted.

units.why: "Instructors may either allow or disallow GenAI tools based on their assessment of the pedagogical value" hands the decision to each instructor (P04).
units.anchor: Instructors may either allow or disallow GenAI tools based on their assessment of the pedagogical
units.policy: Instructors may either allow or disallow GenAI tools based on their assessment of the pedagogical value of these tools within their course.

units.why: "Dartmouth assumes the general rule that GenAI tools are disallowed by default in courses" states what applies absent an instructor decision, a fallback rule (P06) with restrictive effect.
units.anchor: Dartmouth assumes the general rule that GenAI tools are disallowed by default in courses
units.policy: GenAI tools are disallowed by default in courses, so that instructors have full autonomy over how far they allow them.

units.why: "Instructors are encouraged to define AI policies specific to their courses" asks instructors to set course-level rules; P04 (instructor sets rule) rather than P09 because it is not yet about the syllabus, which comes next.
units.anchor: Instructors are encouraged to define AI policies specific to their courses.

units.why: "Dartmouth encourages and supports faculty in exploring innovative learning methods and making use of GenAI tools" is institutional support for faculty experimenting with AI (P63).
units.anchor: Dartmouth encourages and supports faculty in exploring innovative learning methods and making use of GenAI
units.policy: Dartmouth encourages and supports faculty in exploring innovative learning methods and making use of GenAI tools.

units.why: "utilizing these tools may not be the best choice in every course or for every assignment" says AI suitability varies by course and assignment, i.e. a per-instructor/assignment decision (P04).
units.anchor: utilizing these tools may not be the best choice in every course or for every
units.policy: utilizing these tools may not be the best choice in every course or for every assignment

units.why: "Faculty are strongly encouraged to define their GenAI policies in their syllabus" is a recommendation (should) to state AI expectations in the syllabus (P09).
units.anchor: Faculty are strongly encouraged to define their GenAI policies in their syllabus.

units.why: "the instructor's GenAI policy defines the expectations for faculty, students, and staff for that course" makes each instructor's policy govern only that course (P11).
units.anchor: the instructor's GenAI policy defines the expectations for faculty, students, and staff for that course

units.why: "These course policies derive from the Academic Honor Principle" and are "governed by the institutional commitment to Academic Honor", tying course AI rules to the integrity framework (P36 over P56 because it places violations under honor processes).
units.anchor: These course policies derive from the Academic Honor Principle and school Academic Honor Policies

units.why: "the use of these tools is subject to the Academic Honor Policy" means improper permitted use is handled as an honor matter (P36).
units.anchor: Whenever GenAI tools are permitted within a course, the use of these tools is subject
units.policy: Whenever GenAI tools are permitted within a course, the use of these tools is subject to the Academic Honor Policy.

units.why: The sentence explains that GenAI is "not stable, reproducible" so it is acknowledged differently from conventional sources; it is background on disclosure (P24), informational.
units.anchor: As GenAI applications are not stable, reproducible sources, in most cases use of these tools
units.policy: As GenAI applications are not stable, reproducible sources, in most cases use of these tools will not be referenced or cited in the same way as conventional scholarly sources.

units.why: "Students should make sure to confirm appropriate disclosure or acknowledgement methods with their instructors" sets a disclosure-method duty (P24); P10 is about whether use is allowed, which is a different sentence.
units.anchor: Students should make sure to confirm appropriate disclosure or acknowledgement methods with their instructors and
units.policy: Students should make sure to confirm appropriate disclosure or acknowledgement methods with their instructors and follow any provided guidelines.

units.why: "students are expected to use a discipline-appropriate citation method to cite or acknowledge GenAI" is the fallback disclosure rule when the instructor gives none (P24).
units.anchor: students are expected to use a discipline-appropriate citation method to cite or acknowledge GenAI in
units.policy: students are expected to use a discipline-appropriate citation method to cite or acknowledge GenAI in their work

units.why: "Failure to acknowledge or cite GenAI use may result in disciplinary action" makes nondisclosure itself the violation (P28).
units.anchor: Failure to acknowledge or cite GenAI use may result in disciplinary action.

units.why: "they are expected to ask their instructors for clarification" when unsure about acceptable GenAI use is the ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: they are expected to ask their instructors for clarification

units.why: The sentence "Failure to clarify course expectations is not an acceptable justification for violating the Academic Honor Policy" removes ignorance as an excuse; it is about misconduct handling (P36), not the ask-first duty (P10).
units.anchor: Failure to clarify course expectations is not an acceptable justification for violating the Academic Honor
units.policy: Failure to clarify course expectations is not an acceptable justification for violating the Academic Honor Policy.

units.why: The sample statement "This essay was proofread with the assistance of Claude ... The following prompt was used" models acknowledgement that names the tool and the prompt (P25).
units.anchor: The following prompt was used: "Please identify any typographical or grammatical errors in the following
units.policy: The sample acknowledgment statement names the tool (Claude via DartmouthChat), the use (proofreading), and the prompt used.

units.why: The sample citation gives model, version, vendor, date and URL ("Claude 3.5 Haiku, 2024-10-22 version, Anthropic, 29 Aug. 2025"), the details-in-citation pattern (P25).
units.anchor: Claude 3.5 Haiku, 2024-10-22 version, Anthropic, 29 Aug. 2025, chat.dartmouth.edu.

units.why: The sample statement "The code and visualizations ... initially created with assistance from ChatGPT 5 ... reviewed and edited by the author" shows disclosure of AI-created code with a link to the generated content (P24; it is not placed at a code location so not P27).
units.anchor: has been reviewed and edited by the author of this project
units.policy: A sample acknowledgment discloses that code and visualizations were initially created with ChatGPT 5, links the generated content, and says the author reviewed and edited it.

units.why: The sample acknowledgement "I used DartmouthChat and OpenAI's GPT-5 model to generate an outline, which I revised" shows the college's own chat tool in use (P17) as an accepted route; informs only.
units.anchor: I used DartmouthChat and OpenAI's GPT-5 model to generate an outline

documents.unit: Dartmouth Center for the Advancement of Learning
documents.title: Teaching and GenAI: Policies and Guidance
documents.summary: Teaching-center hub that lists staff and student policy links, redesigned Dartmouth assignments from a GenAI teaching grant, and example syllabus statements (some from other institutions) spanning prohibit, restrict and permit. It supports instructors rather than setting rules.
documents.stance_why: The teaching-center page sets no stance of its own; it points to the college policy and offers example Dartmouth assignments and example syllabus statements that range from prohibition (Coffey) to encouragement (Hays), leaving the decision to instructors.

units.why: The hub description says DCAL and Learning Design "share pathways to practical guidance" from "developing course policies to redesigning assignments", i.e. staff support for instructors learning to set AI policy (P63).
units.anchor: From developing course policies to redesigning assignments, Dartmouth's DCAL and Learning Design & Innovation teams
units.policy: From developing course policies to redesigning assignments, Dartmouth's DCAL and Learning Design & Innovation teams share pathways to practical guidance

units.why: "Fifteen Dartmouth educators spent two days in July 2025 participating in the Teaching with GenAI Institute—experimenting, redesigning assignments" describes a faculty-development program (P63).
units.anchor: Fifteen Dartmouth educators spent two days in July 2025 participating in the Teaching with GenAI
units.policy: Fifteen Dartmouth educators took part in a two-day Teaching with GenAI Institute in July 2025 to experiment, redesign assignments, and build strategies for the AI age.

units.why: The page says its example activities "were redesigned under the GenAI Teaching Grant", showing the college funds assignment redesign around AI (P35).
units.anchor: These assignments were redesigned under the
units.policy: Example course assignments were redesigned under the GenAI Teaching Grant and are shared with the grantees' permission.

units.why: In the Art History example students "conduct a close visual analysis ... and then prompt an AI chatbot to analyze the same image" and compare, an assignment built around AI use (P35); the student does their own analysis first.
units.anchor: then prompt an AI chatbot to analyze the same image
units.policy: Art history students first do their own close visual analysis of a photograph, then prompt an AI chatbot to analyze the same image and compare the two interpretations in an essay.

units.why: In the Geography example students are told to document "how they integrated GenAI into their research process", a process-documentation duty (P26).
units.anchor: while documenting how they integrated GenAI into their research process
units.policy: Students create summary reports on NGOs while documenting how they integrated GenAI into their research process.

units.why: "Students could choose to use GenAI as a creative tool, but not as a substitute for their own work" keeps the student as the primary maker (P32); P19 is used for the concrete banned example below.
units.anchor: Students could choose to use GenAI as a creative tool, but not as a substitute
units.policy: Students could choose to use GenAI as a creative tool, but not as a substitute for their own work.

units.why: "prompting AI to write a complete song about Pluto was unacceptable" is a concrete case of having AI produce the submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: prompting AI to write a complete song about Pluto was unacceptable
units.policy: Prompting AI to write a complete song about Pluto is unacceptable.

units.why: The same sentence allows "using AI to generate illustrations for a student-written children's book (with the student responsible for ensuring the images' accuracy)". No type covers permitted AI image generation for a creative project, and P16 is limited to code, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: using AI to generate illustrations for a student-written children's book
units.policy: Using AI to generate illustrations for a student-written children's book is allowed, with the student responsible for ensuring the images' accuracy.
units.uncovered_note: Permitted AI generation of images/illustrations for a creative course project (non-code, non-prose).

units.why: "Students who chose the creative project submitted documentation in stages—brainstorming notes, proposal/outline, and scientific explanations" is staged process evidence of AI integration (P26).
units.anchor: Students who chose the creative project submitted documentation in stages
units.policy: Students who choose the creative project submit documentation in stages (brainstorming notes, proposal/outline, scientific explanations), which shows their process and any AI integration.

units.why: An "A/B analysis revealed that students who read articles before using GenAI developed a much deeper understanding of AI's limitations" is evidence about how AI affects learning (P55).
units.anchor: students who read articles before using GenAI developed a much deeper understanding of AI's limitations

units.why: "students received specific guidelines delineating appropriate and inappropriate GenAI use at each project stage" sorts allowed and disallowed uses by stage of the assignment (P05).
units.anchor: students received specific guidelines delineating appropriate and inappropriate GenAI use at each project stage

units.why: Students in the Design Thinking course valued AI "to jumpstart brainstorming sessions when they felt stuck", an allowed brainstorming use (P15).
units.anchor: particularly valuing its ability to jumpstart brainstorming sessions when they felt stuck

units.why: The Writing course had students use AI as a Socratic questioner that never gives analysis, and "This was the only permitted GenAI use in the course", i.e. a sanctioned tutor-like use (P12) with all other use disallowed.
units.anchor: This was the only permitted GenAI use in the course.
units.policy: In Writing 2/3, using GenAI as a Socratic questioner (structured prompt, questions only, no analysis) is the only permitted GenAI use.

units.why: In the CS course Singh "asked students to engage with at least one GenAI system" (ChatGPT, GitHub Copilot, multimodal models) and reflect, so AI use is required work (P02).
units.anchor: asked students to engage with at least one GenAI system
units.policy: In a Human-Centered Generative AI computer science course, students engage with at least one GenAI system and connect the experience to course readings.

units.why: "the course developed critical GenAI literacy essential for future AI developers" frames the CS reflection assignment as teaching AI use as a professional skill (P44).
units.anchor: the course developed critical GenAI literacy essential for future AI developers

units.why: Offshore Wind students "regularly queried industry visitors/speakers about workplace GenAI use", connecting the course to professional AI practice (P44).
units.anchor: Students regularly queried industry visitors/speakers about workplace GenAI use and anticipated developments.

units.why: "Offshore Wind Power students used GenAI to summarize lengthy documents" for project wiki pages is a sanctioned summarizing/study use (P14).
units.anchor: Offshore Wind Power students used GenAI to summarize lengthy documents
units.policy: Offshore Wind Power students use GenAI to summarize lengthy documents for integration into project Wiki pages.

units.why: Geovisualization students first code "by hand in Leaflet.js to understand fundamental mechanics" and only then "progressed to using GenAI", a staged permission (P08).
units.anchor: After initially coding by hand in Leaflet.js to understand fundamental mechanics
units.policy: Geovisualization students code by hand first to understand fundamentals, then progress to using GenAI for narrow coding problems and for generating complete web map applications.

units.why: The coding assignment "required learning to formulate effective prompts ... and critically evaluate AI outputs", teaching students to check AI code (P31).
units.anchor: This required learning to formulate effective prompts, identify issues, iterate solutions, and critically evaluate AI
units.policy: This required learning to formulate effective prompts, identify issues, iterate solutions, and critically evaluate AI outputs.

units.why: "The course integrated discussion of social context and ethical issues surrounding AI use" names ethical concerns as course content (P53).
units.anchor: The course integrated discussion of social context and ethical issues surrounding AI use

units.why: "Graded on completion to encourage honest experimentation" changes the grading scheme so students can experiment with AI openly (P35).
units.anchor: Graded on completion to encourage honest experimentation
units.policy: The low-stakes GenAI content-analysis assignment is graded on completion to encourage honest experimentation.

units.why: "One Spanish-language learner benefited significantly from AI as a language-translation tool" reports translation as a useful use of AI on texts, a prose/language use separate from code (P18).
units.anchor: One Spanish-language learner benefited significantly from AI as a language-translation tool.

units.why: The example notes "inferior free models" as a constraint, a mention of unequal access between free and paid models (P51); it only informs.
units.anchor: Technical constraints (token limits, inferior free models) became lessons about AI infrastructure's impact on research.

units.why: "The introductory titles for these summaries were developed with assistance from Claude Sonnet 4.5, accessed through Dartmouth Chat" is the center's own disclosure of AI use in its materials (P48) and names the sanctioned tool.
units.anchor: The introductory titles for these summaries were developed with assistance from Claude Sonnet 4.5
units.policy: The introductory titles for the example summaries were developed with assistance from Claude Sonnet 4.5, accessed through Dartmouth Chat.

units.why: In the Boke anthropology example, "I ask that you do not use AI generators to create work unless specifically requested to" bans AI-produced work (P19).
units.anchor: I ask that you do not use AI generators to create work unless specifically requested
units.policy: I ask that you do not use AI generators to create work unless specifically requested to.

units.why: Boke's statement says "We will be working directly with AI writing tools several times through the semester ... and citing them appropriately", course-directed AI use with citation (P24 for the citation duty; the use itself is in-class).
units.anchor: We will be working directly with AI writing tools several times through the semester
units.policy: Students work directly with AI writing tools several times in the semester, exploring their opportunities and weaknesses, and cite them appropriately.

units.why: Coffey's art history statement ends its argument with "I do not permit AI writing supports in this class", a course-level ban on AI for writing (P01).
units.anchor: I do not permit AI writing supports in this class.

units.why: Coffey says AI writing supports are "short-circuiting the necessary relationship between thinking, writing, and learning", the argument that AI shortcuts practice (P41).
units.anchor: short-circuiting the necessary relationship between thinking, writing, and learning

units.why: "AI produces banal texts that are often repetitive and riddled with inaccuracies" warns that output is unreliable (P31).
units.anchor: AI produces banal texts that are often repetitive and riddled with inaccuracies.

units.why: "AI writing tools plagiarize the work of scholars without their consent" is an ethical/IP objection to AI (P53).
units.anchor: AI writing tools plagiarize the work of scholars without their consent and without any concern
units.policy: AI writing tools plagiarize the work of scholars without their consent and without any concern for citation.

units.why: Coffey separates "AI reading and research supports" and says "It is permissible to use, for example, google translate" to read Spanish articles; P18 covers language tools distinct from writing support, and the ban stays for writing.
units.anchor: It is permissible to use, for example, google translate—in this class only—to read articles originally
units.policy: It is permissible to use, for example, google translate—in this class only—to read articles originally published in Spanish.

units.why: "you may not ask ChatGPT or any other AI program to generate a bibliography for you" bans AI-generated submitted content (P19).
units.anchor: you may not ask ChatGPT or any other AI program to generate a bibliography for
units.policy: you may not ask ChatGPT or any other AI program to generate a bibliography for you

units.why: "You may not use grammerly's AI function or ChatGPT or any other LLM to edit your writing, fix your grammar and spelling errors" bans AI proofreading of graded work (P21).
units.anchor: You may not use grammerly's AI function or ChatGPT or any other LLM to edit
units.policy: You may not use grammerly's AI function or ChatGPT or any other LLM to edit your writing

units.why: "You may use word or google doc's basic spell and grammar checks" permits non-generative checking in prose work (P18).
units.anchor: You may use word or google doc's basic spell and grammar checks.

units.why: "If you are using an AI program that I have not mentioned here, you MUST not use it in this class unless you inquire with me beforehand" sets the rule for unlisted tools, a fallback (P06).
units.anchor: you MUST not use it in this class unless you inquire with me beforehand
units.policy: An AI program not mentioned in the policy must not be used unless the student inquires with the instructor beforehand.

units.why: "What I may accept, another professor might not and vice versa" tells students this course's AI rules are specific to this class (P11).
units.anchor: What I may accept, another professor might not and vice versa.

units.why: "When in doubt, ASK first. Permission will not be granted ex post facto." is the ask-before-using rule (P10).
units.anchor: When in doubt, ASK first. Permission will not be granted ex post facto.

units.why: "I will first call you in for a conference to discuss my concerns" means talking with the student before consequences (P57).
units.anchor: If I determine that you have used AI writing supports of any kind, I will
units.policy: If the instructor determines a student used AI writing supports, the instructor first calls the student in for a conference to discuss concerns and determine consequences.

units.why: "consequences which can range from failure of the individual assignment to failure of the class and a formal report to the Committee on Standards" states penalties in advance (P37).
units.anchor: consequences which can range from failure of the individual assignment to failure of the class
units.policy: Consequences for AI writing support use range from failure of the individual assignment to failure of the class and a formal report to the Committee on Standards.

units.why: "submitting work, of ANY KIND, that is not your own is CHEATING and will result in failing the class" classes it as cheating with a set penalty (P36 chosen as the primary type; the penalty is part of the same sentence).
units.anchor: submitting work, of ANY KIND, that is not your own is CHEATING and will result
units.policy: submitting work, of ANY KIND, that is not your own is CHEATING and will result in failing the class.

units.why: "They evolve and change, and your honest input can impact how they do" says the policy will change and invites feedback (P54).
units.anchor: They evolve and change, and your honest input can impact how they do.

units.why: Benor's statement says "Assume the output is incorrect unless you check the claims with reliable sources", a verify-output duty (P31).
units.anchor: Assume the output is incorrect unless you check the claims with reliable sources.

units.why: "Their output may reflect bias because the data they are trained on may reflect bias" names bias in AI output (P53).
units.anchor: Their output may reflect bias because the data they are trained on may reflect bias

units.why: "you are welcome to use AI generators to brainstorm and refine ideas, find reliable sources, outline, check grammar" lists several allowed uses; P15 chosen because brainstorming and outlining lead the list, and P18 (prose) is the other candidate.
units.anchor: you are welcome to use AI generators to brainstorm and refine ideas, find reliable sources,
units.policy: Students are welcome to use AI generators to brainstorm and refine ideas, find reliable sources, outline, check grammar, refine wording, and format bibliographies.

units.why: "Beyond bibliographies, you are not allowed to copy and paste material generated by AI and use it in your assignments" bans AI-generated text as submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: you are not allowed to copy and paste material generated by AI and use it
units.policy: you are not allowed to copy and paste material generated by AI and use it in your assignments

units.why: "add a note indicating which AI tool you used and how you used it, including the prompt(s) you used and the date(s)" requires tool, prompt and date in the disclosure (P25).
units.anchor: add a note indicating which AI tool you used and how you used it, including
units.policy: add a note indicating which AI tool you used and how you used it, including the prompt(s) you used and the date(s)

units.why: Goodman says "I would prefer you not use these tools and instead commit to the productive struggle that is learning" but does not ban them, so AI is discouraged, not forbidden (P03).
units.anchor: While I would prefer you not use these tools and instead commit to the productive
units.policy: The instructor would prefer students not use these tools and commit to the productive struggle of learning, but does not ban them.

units.why: "Rather than ban them, we will treat them similarly to other resources you use" treats AI like any other resource under existing rules (P45).
units.anchor: Rather than ban them, we will treat them similarly to other resources you use.

units.why: "Give notice that you used the AI tool, which one you used and how you used it in the comments of your code" marks AI use at the place in the code (P27).
units.anchor: Give notice that you used the AI tool, which one you used and how you
units.policy: Give notice that you used the AI tool, which one you used and how you used it in the comments of your code.

units.why: "Rigorously test and alter the program to suit the assignment and your understanding" requires checking and adapting AI-produced code (P31).
units.anchor: Rigorously test and alter the program to suit the assignment and your understanding.

units.why: "You must understand any code you submit and be prepared to explain it to me" is the explain-every-line duty (P30).
units.anchor: You must understand any code you submit and be prepared to explain it to me.

units.why: "All comments should be your own words" sets a prose rule for code comments separate from the code rules (P18).
units.anchor: All comments should be your own words.

units.why: "the following course policies are provisional and subject to change" is an explicit statement that the policy will be revisited (P54).
units.anchor: the following course policies are provisional and subject to change

units.why: "If you outsource your homework to a chatbot, you will risk diminishing your own learning experience" says AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: If you outsource your homework to a chatbot, you will risk diminishing your own learning
units.policy: If you outsource your homework to a chatbot, you will risk diminishing your own learning experience.

units.why: "GenAI is not beholden to the truth" and "is telling you something that might sound right" warns that output may be wrong (P31).
units.anchor: GenAI is not beholden to the truth.

units.why: "Use of GenAI on written assignments is permitted at your discretion, provided that it is judiciously implemented and reviewed, and properly documented" is a default permission with conditions for written work (P02; also prose-specific P18 but the permission is the main point).
units.anchor: Use of GenAI on written assignments is permitted at your discretion, provided that it is
units.policy: Use of GenAI on written assignments is permitted at the student's discretion, provided that it is judiciously implemented and reviewed, and properly documented at the time of submission.

units.why: "you must turn in a cover letter ... a comprehensive and verbatim list of the prompts you used, and a note on how you checked the accuracy" requires reflection plus prompt log with each AI-assisted assignment (P26).
units.anchor: you must turn in a cover letter, including an explanation of your strategy and reasoning
units.policy: For any assignment on which GenAI is used, students must turn in a cover letter explaining their strategy and reasoning, a comprehensive and verbatim list of prompts, and a note on how they checked the accuracy of the output.

units.why: "You are responsible for what you turn in for assessment, including any inaccuracies or factual errors" makes students own their submissions (P29).
units.anchor: You are responsible for what you turn in for assessment, including any inaccuracies or factual
units.policy: You are responsible for what you turn in for assessment, including any inaccuracies or factual errors in the text.

units.why: "If you are uncertain about whether a particular application of GenAI complies with our course policies ... please get in touch with me" is ask-first (P10).
units.anchor: If you are uncertain about whether a particular application of GenAI complies with our course
units.policy: Students uncertain whether a particular application of GenAI complies with the course policies should get in touch with the instructor.

units.why: Notareschi's statement requires "an Artificial Intelligence Disclosure" in every paper, an AI disclosure with each submission (P24); the sentence states two required features.
units.anchor: every paper should have two features indicating our reliance on outside sources
units.policy: Every paper has a citation list and an Artificial Intelligence Disclosure stating whether AI was used and how.

units.why: The disclosure checklist lists the "acceptable uses": brainstorming, outlining, background information, grammar/spelling help. P15 chosen as the first listed; a list of uses, not one type, so P15 with brainstorming/outlining as the core.
units.anchor: Brainstorming help Outlining help Background information Grammar/spelling/punctuation/mechanics help
units.policy: The acceptable uses of AI are brainstorming help, outlining help, background information, and grammar/spelling/punctuation/mechanics help.

units.why: Students must "affirm I did not generate text with artificial intelligence and directly copy it into my paper", banning pasting AI text as submitted work (P19).
units.anchor: I affirm I did not generate text with artificial intelligence and directly copy it into
units.policy: I affirm I did not generate text with artificial intelligence and directly copy it into my paper.

units.why: Copying AI words "would be considered plagiarism", classing it as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: this would be considered plagiarism (which means presenting others' words as if they were our
units.policy: this would be considered plagiarism (which means presenting others' words as if they were our own)

units.why: "using AI to generate text may rob us of the chance to develop our own thinking" is the skill-building rationale (P41).
units.anchor: using AI to generate text may rob us of the chance to develop our own
units.policy: using AI to generate text may rob us of the chance to develop our own thinking on a subject

units.why: "AI engines reproduce biases and prejudices ... it is incumbent on us to check and correct for bias" names bias and asks users to check (P53).
units.anchor: it is incumbent on us to check and correct for bias

units.why: Joubin's statement says using an AI generator "without proper attribution violates academic integrity", treating undisclosed use as misconduct (P36).
units.anchor: Using an AI-content generator such as ChatGPT to complete assignments without proper attribution violates academic
units.policy: Using an AI-content generator such as ChatGPT to complete assignments without proper attribution violates academic integrity.

units.why: "Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is an important skill in today's society" is the professional-skill rationale (P44).
units.anchor: Learning to use AI responsibly and ethically is an important skill in today's society.

units.why: "Fact-check all of the AI outputs. Assume it is wrong unless you cross-check" requires verification (P31).
units.anchor: Fact-check all of the AI outputs.

units.why: "write a short paragraph to explain which AI tool and how you used it ... Include the prompts you used" requires tool and prompt in the disclosure (P25).
